title: Nehemiah

stories.title: 🙏 Nehemiah 1
summaryBullets: These are the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah: In the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, while I was in the citadel of Susa, (1:1).
Hanani, one of my brothers, arrived with men from Judah. So I questioned them about the remnant of the Jews who had survived the exile, and also about Jerusalem. (1:2).
And they told me, “The remnant who survived the exile are there in the province, in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire.” (1:3).
When I heard these words, I sat down and wept. I mourned for days, fasting and praying before the God of heaven. (1:4).
Then I said: “O LORD, God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion with those who love Him and keep His commandments, (1:5).

let Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive to hear the prayer that I, Your servant, now pray before You day and night for Your servants, the Israelites. I confess the sins that we Israelites have committed against You. Both I and my father’s house have sinned. (1:6).
We have behaved corruptly against You and have not kept the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that You gave Your servant Moses. (1:7).
Remember, I pray, the word that You commanded Your servant Moses when You said, ‘If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the nations, (1:8).

but if you return to Me and keep and practice My commandments, then even if your exiles have been banished to the farthest horizon, I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I have chosen as a dwelling for My Name.’ (1:9).
They are Your servants and Your people. You redeemed them by Your great power and mighty hand. (1:10).

O Lord, may Your ear be attentive to my prayer and to the prayers of Your servants who delight to revere Your name. Give Your servant success this day, I pray, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” (At that time I was the cupbearer to the king.) (1:11).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 36:15-21: Jerusalem's wall is broken down and the city burned, and the land keeps its sabbaths seventy years.
Deuteronomy 30:1-5: If you return to Me, I will gather you from the farthest horizon, the promise Nehemiah quotes back to God.
1 Kings 8:46-53: Solomon asks God to hear from heaven when the people repent in the land of their captors.
Daniel 9:4-19: A confession in exile that owns the nation's guilt and appeals to God's covenant love.
Ezra 4:17-23: The order of Artaxerxes that stopped the work by force, leaving the wall broken and the gates burned.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַשְׁקֶה (mashqeh, one who gives drink)
translationNotes.note: Not a waiter. The cupbearer poured the king's wine and drank a little first in front of him, which made him the last line of defence against poison and put him in the king's private company every day. The office went to trusted nobles: Pharaoh had one (Genesis 40:1-13), and Assyria's Rabshakeh, the officer who negotiated under Jerusalem's wall in 2 Kings 18, carries a title meaning chief cupbearer. Nehemiah's job is why a provincial rebuilding project could be settled in one conversation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּסְלֵו (Kislev)
translationNotes.note: Kislev is the ninth month, mid-November to mid-December, when the winter rains set in. The twentieth year is the twentieth of Artaxerxes I, which puts this in late 446 or 445 BC, about ninety years after the first exiles went home under Cyrus and roughly thirteen years after Ezra's caravan arrived.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוּשַׁן הַבִּירָה (Shushan habbirah)
translationNotes.note: Birah means the fortified palace compound, not the town. Susa lay in what is now southwestern Iran, and the Persian court wintered there; the acropolis mound held Darius' audience hall and the royal apartments, walled off above the city below. The same phrase is the setting of the book of Esther, and Nehemiah is standing in it about thirty-five years later.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם (elohei hashamayim)
translationNotes.note: The standard way Judeans named the LORD in Persian-period public and official speech, running through Ezra, Nehemiah and Daniel (Ezra 1:2; 7:12; Daniel 2:18). It states that their God is not a local deity of one hill country. Nehemiah uses it in prayer before he uses it in front of a king who expects that kind of title.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲנָנִי (Chanani)
translationNotes.note: Nehemiah's own brother, who comes from Judah with men of the province and brings the report that starts the book (1:2). He turns up again at 7:2, when Nehemiah puts him in charge of Jerusalem alongside the commander of the citadel. The news travels by family, and the man who carried it ends up governing the city.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nehemiah learns of Jerusalem’s ruin, mourns, and prays for God’s mercy and favor before the king.

stories.title: 👑 Nehemiah 2
summaryBullets: Now in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was set before him, I took the wine and gave it to the king. I had never been sad in his presence, (2:1).
so the king said to me, “Why is your face sad, though you are not ill? This could only be sadness of the heart.” I was overwhelmed with fear (2:2).
and replied to the king, “May the king live forever! Why should I not be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?” (2:3).
“What is your request?” replied the king. So I prayed to the God of heaven (2:4).

and answered the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, I ask that you send me to Judah, to the city where my fathers are buried, so that I may rebuild it.” (2:5).
Then the king, with the queen seated beside him, asked me, “How long will your journey take, and when will you return?” So it pleased the king to send me, and I set a time. (2:6).
I also said to him, “If it pleases the king, may letters be given to me for the governors west of the Euphrates, so that they will grant me safe passage until I reach Judah. (2:7).

And may I have a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest, so that he will give me timber to make beams for the gates of the citadel to the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I will occupy.” And because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests. (2:8).
Then I went to the governors west of the Euphrates and gave them the king’s letters. The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me. (2:9).
But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard about this, they were deeply disturbed that someone had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites. (2:10).
After I had arrived in Jerusalem and had been there three days, (2:11).
I set out at night with a few men. I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem. The only animal with me was the one on which I was riding. (2:12).

So I went out at night through the Valley Gate toward the Well of the Serpent and the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that had been broken down and the gates that had been destroyed by fire. (2:13).
Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool, but there was no room for the animal under me to get through; (2:14).
so I went up the valley by night and inspected the wall. Then I headed back and reentered through the Valley Gate. (2:15).
The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, for I had not yet told the Jews or priests or nobles or officials or any other workers. (2:16).

Then I said to them, “You see the trouble we are in. Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned down. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace.” (2:17).
I also told them about the gracious hand of my God upon me, and what the king had said to me. “Let us start rebuilding,” they replied, and they set their hands to this good work. (2:18).

But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and Geshem the Arab heard about this, they mocked us and ridiculed us, saying, “What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?” (2:19).
So I answered them and said, “The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success. We, His servants, will start rebuilding, but you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.” (2:20).
crossRefs: Ezra 7:11-26: The same king writes a letter of authority and funding for Ezra a few years earlier.
Psalm 102:13-17: The LORD's servants take pleasure in Zion's stones and have pity on her dust, and He builds up Zion.
Esther 4:1-2: No one may enter the king's gate in sackcloth, which is why grief in the palace was dangerous.
2 Chronicles 32:2-5: Hezekiah repairs the broken wall of Jerusalem, raises towers on it and builds another wall outside.
Nehemiah 3:1-32: The gate-by-gate record of the repairs Nehemiah organises after this night ride.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רַע פָּנִים (ra panim, bad of face)
translationNotes.note: Nehemiah says he had never been sad before the king, and that when the king noticed he was very much afraid (2:1-2). The Persian court was a controlled space where mood was part of protocol; Esther 4:2 records the rule that nobody could even enter the king's gate wearing sackcloth. A servant showing grief could look like a servant with a grievance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פַּרְדֵּס (pardes) - Greek: παράδεισος (paradeisos)
translationNotes.note: Pardes is a Persian loanword for a walled royal park or timber preserve, and it is the word Greek borrowed as paradeisos and English as paradise. Asaph is its keeper, a crown officer over a resource the crown controlled, so beams for the citadel gates and the city gates had to be signed out by letter (2:8). The wood was not for sale on any market.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וָאֵצְאָה בְשַׁעַר־הַגַּיְא לָיְלָה (va-etse'ah be-sha'ar hagai laylah, I went out by night through the Valley Gate)
translationNotes.note: He rides out at night by the Valley Gate on the west, past the Dragon Spring to the Dung Gate on the south, on to the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, and up the Kidron ravine on the east (2:13-15). It is a survey of the weakest side of the city, made in the dark with no officials watching. At one point the rubble was so deep his mount could not get through and he went on foot.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סַנְבַלַּט (Sanvallat) - טוֹבִיָּה (Toviyyah) - גֶּשֶׁם (Geshem)
translationNotes.note: Three neighbouring power-holders, and all three are attested outside Scripture. A letter from the Jewish garrison at Elephantine in Egypt, dated 407 BC, names 'Delaiah and Shelemiah, the sons of Sanballat governor of Samaria'. A silver bowl from Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt, now in the Brooklyn Museum, is inscribed for 'Qainu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar', the spelling Nehemiah 6:6 uses. The Tobiad family later held the estate at Iraq al-Amir in Jordan, where the name Tobiah is carved in Aramaic letters at the caves.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַחֹרֹנִי (ha-Choroni) - הָעֶבֶד הָעַמֹּנִי (ha-eved ha-Ammoni) - הָעַרְבִי (ha-Arvi)
translationNotes.note: The three titles map the compass around Judah: Sanballat from Beth-horon or Horonaim, tied to Samaria in the north; Tobiah called 'the servant', meaning a Persian official, over Ammon across the Jordan to the east; Geshem heading the Qedarite Arab confederation to the south and east. A walled Jerusalem sat in the middle of all three men's trade and tax interests.

translationNotes.term: No portion, right, or memorial in Jerusalem
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵלֶק וּצְדָקָה וְזִכָּרוֹן (cheleq u-tsedaqah ve-zikkaron)
translationNotes.note: Nehemiah's answer in 2:20 uses three legal words: a share in the property, a recognised claim, and a recorded memorial or precedent. He is not insulting them; he is telling them they have no standing in the case. Persian provincial disputes were fought exactly on those grounds.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nehemiah receives the king’s support, inspects Jerusalem’s ruined walls, and rallies the people to rebuild despite mockery.

stories.title: 🧱 Nehemiah 3
summaryBullets: At the Sheep Gate, Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests began rebuilding. They dedicated it and installed its doors. After building as far as the Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel, they dedicated the wall. (3:1).
The men of Jericho built next to Eliashib, and Zaccur son of Imri built next to them. (3:2).
The Fish Gate was rebuilt by the sons of Hassenaah. They laid its beams and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. (3:3).

Next to them, Meremoth son of Uriah, the son of Hakkoz, made repairs. Next to him, Meshullam son of Berechiah, the son of Meshezabel, made repairs; and next to him, Zadok son of Baana made repairs as well. (3:4).
Next to him, the Tekoites made repairs, but their nobles did not put their shoulders to the work under their supervisors. (3:5).
The Jeshanah Gate was repaired by Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah. They laid its beams and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. (3:6).

Next to them, repairs were made by Melatiah the Gibeonite, Jadon the Meronothite, and the men of Gibeon and Mizpah, who were under the authority of the governor of the region west of the Euphrates. (3:7).
Next to them, Uzziel son of Harhaiah, one of the goldsmiths, made repairs. And next to him, Hananiah, one of the perfumers, made repairs. They fortified Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall. (3:8).
Next to them, Rephaiah son of Hur, ruler of a half-district of Jerusalem, made repairs; (3:9).
next to him, Jedaiah son of Harumaph made repairs across from his house; and next to him, Hattush son of Hashabneiah made repairs. (3:10).
Malchijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahath-moab repaired another section, as well as the Tower of the Ovens. (3:11).
And next to them, Shallum son of Hallohesh, ruler of the other half-district of Jerusalem, made repairs, with the help of his daughters. (3:12).
The Valley Gate was repaired by Hanun and the residents of Zanoah. They rebuilt it, installed its doors, bolts, and bars, and repaired a thousand cubits of the wall as far as the Dung Gate. (3:13).
The Dung Gate was repaired by Malchijah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem. He rebuilt it and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. (3:14).

The Fountain Gate was repaired by Shallun son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah. He rebuilt it, roofed it, and installed its doors, bolts, and bars. He also repaired the wall of the Pool of Shelah near the king’s garden, as far as the stairs that descend from the City of David. (3:15).
Beyond him, Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of a half-district of Beth-zur, made repairs up to a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the artificial pool and the House of the Mighty. (3:16).
Next to him, the Levites made repairs under Rehum son of Bani, and next to him, Hashabiah, ruler of a half-district of Keilah, made repairs for his district. (3:17).
Next to him, their countrymen made repairs under Binnui son of Henadad, ruler of the other half-district of Keilah. (3:18).
And next to him, Ezer son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section opposite the ascent to the armory, near the angle in the wall. (3:19).
Next to him, Baruch son of Zabbai diligently repaired another section, from the angle to the doorway of the house of Eliashib the high priest. (3:20).
Next to him, Meremoth son of Uriah, the son of Hakkoz, repaired another section, from the doorway of the house of Eliashib to the end of the house. (3:21).
And next to him, the priests from the surrounding area made repairs. (3:22).
Beyond them, Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs in front of their house, and next to them, Azariah son of Maaseiah, the son of Ananiah, made repairs beside his house. (3:23).
After him, Binnui son of Henadad repaired another section, from the house of Azariah to the angle and the corner, (3:24).
and Palal son of Uzai made repairs opposite the angle and the tower that juts out from the upper palace of the king near the courtyard of the guard. Next to him, Pedaiah son of Parosh (3:25).
and the temple servants living on the hill of Ophel made repairs opposite the Water Gate toward the east and the tower that juts out. (3:26).
And next to them, the Tekoites repaired another section, from a point opposite the great tower that juts out to the wall of Ophel. (3:27).
Above the Horse Gate, each of the priests made repairs in front of his own house. (3:28).
Next to them, Zadok son of Immer made repairs opposite his house, and next to him, Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, the guard of the East Gate, made repairs. (3:29).
Next to him, Hananiah son of Shelemiah, as well as Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another section. Next to them, Meshullam son of Berechiah made repairs opposite his own quarters. (3:30).

Next to him, Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths, made repairs as far as the house of the temple servants and the merchants, opposite the Inspection Gate, and as far as the upper room above the corner. (3:31).
And between the upper room above the corner and the Sheep Gate, the goldsmiths and merchants made repairs. (3:32).
crossRefs: Nehemiah 12:27-43: Two choirs walk this same circuit in opposite directions at the dedication of the finished wall.
2 Kings 14:13: Jehoash breaks down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.
2 Chronicles 26:9: Uzziah builds towers at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate and the Angle, and fortifies them.
Jeremiah 31:38-40: The city will be rebuilt from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate and around to the Horse Gate.
John 5:2: There is a pool in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate, called Bethesda, with five covered colonnades.

translationNotes.term: The gates, in order around the circuit
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁעַר (sha'ar, gate)
translationNotes.note: Every gate is named for what came through it or what stood by it, and the chapter walks them anticlockwise from the temple. Sheep Gate on the north for animals brought to the altar; Fish Gate, where Tyrian traders sold their catch (13:16; Zephaniah 1:10); Old Gate; Valley Gate on the west toward the Hinnom ravine; Dung Gate on the south, where refuse went out; Fountain Gate by the Pool of Siloam and the King's Garden; Water Gate on the east above the Gihon spring; Horse Gate by the palace; East Gate; and the Muster Gate, where troops were inspected.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַחוֹמָה הָרְחָבָה (hachomah harechavah)
translationNotes.note: Named in 3:8 as a known landmark. In 1970 Nahman Avigad uncovered a stretch of city wall in the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem seven metres thick, twenty-three feet, and traced it for sixty-five metres; it dates to the eighth century BC, the generation of Hezekiah and Isaiah. Nehemiah's builders were not drawing a new line, they were repairing one that was already three hundred years old.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶלֶף אַמָּה (elef ammah)
translationNotes.note: In 3:13 Hanun and the people of Zanoah repair the Valley Gate and then a thousand cubits of wall as far as the Dung Gate. A cubit is about eighteen inches, forearm length, so that single stretch runs about 1,500 feet, a quarter of a mile of masonry assigned to one town's work party.

translationNotes.term: The Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִגְדַּל הַמֵּאָה (Migdal Hammeah) - מִגְדַּל חֲנַנְאֵל (Migdal Chananel)
translationNotes.note: Both stand at the north end by the Sheep Gate (3:1), which is the one side of Jerusalem with no ravine under it and therefore the only easy approach for an army. That is why the priests build there first and why the towers are concentrated there. Jeremiah 31:38 and Zechariah 14:10 both use the Tower of Hananel as the northern corner marker of the city.

translationNotes.term: Goldsmiths, perfumers and merchants on the wall
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַצֹּרְפִים (hatsorfim, goldsmiths) - הָרֹקְחִים (haroqchim, perfumers)
translationNotes.note: The work is parcelled out by guild, family and town, and the trade names are precise. The perfumers were the compounders of aromatic oils and incense, the craft regulated in Exodus 30:22-38 for the sanctuary. Jewellers and perfumers rebuilt a defensive wall, and one section was repaired by Shallum and his daughters (3:12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּלֶךְ (pelekh, district)
translationNotes.note: Verses 9 to 19 name the administrative districts of the province and their rulers: Jerusalem, Beth-haccherem, Mizpah, Beth-zur and Keilah, several of them split into halves with a ruler each. This is the Persian province of Yehud on paper, and the wall was built by its local government units. The nobles of Tekoa are singled out at 3:5 for refusing to put their necks to the work of their lords.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nehemiah records the organized work of priests, families, and tradesmen repairing Jerusalem’s gates and walls.

stories.title: ⚔️ Nehemiah 4
summaryBullets: Now when Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he was furious and filled with indignation. He ridiculed the Jews (4:1).

before his associates and the army of Samaria, saying, “What are these feeble Jews doing? Can they restore the wall by themselves? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they complete it in a day? Can they bring these burnt stones back to life from the mounds of rubble?” (4:2).
Then Tobiah the Ammonite, who was beside him, said, “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!” (4:3).
Hear us, O God, for we are despised. Turn their scorn back upon their own heads, and let them be taken as plunder to a land of captivity. (4:4).
Do not cover up their iniquity or let their sin be blotted out from Your sight, for they have provoked the builders. (4:5).
So we rebuilt the wall until all of it was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a mind to work. (4:6).

When Sanballat and Tobiah, together with the Arabs, Ammonites, and Ashdodites, heard that the repair to the walls of Jerusalem was progressing and that the gaps were being closed, they were furious, (4:7).
and all of them conspired to come and fight against Jerusalem and create a hindrance. (4:8).
So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night. (4:9).
Meanwhile, the people of Judah said: “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.” (4:10).
And our enemies said, “Before they know or see a thing, we will come into their midst, kill them, and put an end to the work.” (4:11).
At that time the Jews who lived nearby came and told us ten times over, “Wherever you turn, they will attack us.” (4:12).
So I stationed men behind the lowest sections of the wall, at the vulnerable areas. I stationed them by families with their swords, spears, and bows. (4:13).

After I had made an inspection, I stood up and said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.” (4:14).
When our enemies heard that we were aware of their scheme and that God had frustrated it, each of us returned to his own work on the wall. (4:15).
And from that day on, half of my servants did the work while the other half held spears, shields, bows, and armor. The officers stationed themselves behind all the people of Judah (4:16).
who were rebuilding the wall. The laborers who carried materials worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other. (4:17).
And each of the builders worked with his sword strapped at his side. But the trumpeter stayed beside me. (4:18).
Then I said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people: “The work is great and extensive, and we are spread out far from one another along the wall. (4:19).
Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us!” (4:20).
So we continued the work, while half of the men held spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out. (4:21).
At that time I also said to the people, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem, so that they can stand guard by night and work by day.” (4:22).
So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes; each carried his weapon, even to go for water. (4:23).
crossRefs: Ezra 4:1-5: The same neighbours had already worked to discourage the builders and hire counsellors against them.
Numbers 10:9: When you go to war in your land, sound an alarm with the trumpets and you will be remembered before the LORD.
Psalm 127:1: Unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labour in vain; unless He watches the city, the watchman stays awake for nothing.
2 Chronicles 20:15-17: Do not be afraid of this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God's.
Nehemiah 6:1-14: Once the breaches are closed the same enemies switch from open threat to invitation and forged letters.

translationNotes.term: Stones out of the burnt rubbish heaps
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵעֲרֵמוֹת הֶעָפָר (me-aremot he-afar, from the heaps of dust)
translationNotes.note: Sanballat's jeer in 4:2 is technical, not just abusive: will they bring these stones back to life out of the rubbish heaps, burnt as they are? Jerusalem is built of limestone, and limestone that has been through a fire cracks and crumbles to lime. He is saying the salvage is worthless. They used it anyway.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָאַשְׁדּוֹדִים (ha-Ashdodim)
translationNotes.note: Ashdod was one of the five old Philistine cities, on the coastal plain about thirty-five miles west of Jerusalem, and it was still a distinct people with its own speech in the Persian period; 13:24 complains that children of mixed marriages spoke Ashdodite. With Arabs to the south, Ammonites east, Samaria north and Ashdod west, 4:7-8 has the city ringed on all four sides.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוֹפָר (shofar, ram's horn)
translationNotes.note: The work is spread so thin along the wall that men are out of sight of each other, so Nehemiah keeps the trumpeter at his own side and tells them to rally to the sound (4:18-20). A ram's horn carries for miles across broken ground. Numbers 10:9 is the law he is invoking: sound the alarm and you will be remembered before your God.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹמַח (romach, spear) - שִׁרְיֹן (shiryon, coat of mail)
translationNotes.note: Half the men held spears, shields, bows and body armour while the other half built; the load carriers worked one-handed with a weapon in the other, and the masons kept a sword strapped on (4:16-18). Body armour here is scale armour, bronze or iron plates sewn to a leather coat. Nobody undressed: 4:23 says they did not take off their clothes, each keeping his weapon even at the water.

translationNotes.term: From dawn until the stars came out
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵעֲלוֹת הַשַּׁחַר עַד צֵאת הַכּוֹכָבִים (me-alot hashachar ad tset hakokhavim)
translationNotes.note: The phrase in 4:21 marks a working day from first light to full dark, roughly fourteen hours, and it is the same pair of markers Jewish reckoning uses to open and close a day. Nehemiah also orders everyone to sleep inside Jerusalem rather than go home to the villages, so the night watch had a garrison and the labour force had no commute.

stories.keyTakeaway: The builders defend themselves with weapons in hand while repairing the walls under constant threat.

stories.title: ⚖️ Nehemiah 5
summaryBullets: About that time there was a great outcry from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews. (5:1).
Some were saying, “We and our sons and daughters are numerous. We must get grain in order to eat and stay alive.” (5:2).
Others were saying, “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our homes to get grain during the famine.” (5:3).
Still others were saying, “We have borrowed money to pay the king’s tax on our fields and vineyards. (5:4).

We and our children are just like our countrymen and their children, yet we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery. Some of our daughters are already enslaved, but we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others.” (5:5).
When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I became extremely angry, (5:6).
and after serious thought I rebuked the nobles and officials, saying, “You are exacting usury from your own brothers!” So I called a large assembly against them (5:7).

and said, “We have done our best to buy back our Jewish brothers who were sold to foreigners, but now you are selling your own brothers, that they may be sold back to us!” But they remained silent, for they could find nothing to say. (5:8).
So I continued, “What you are doing is not right. Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies? (5:9).
I, as well as my brothers and my servants, have been lending the people money and grain. Please, let us stop this usury. (5:10).
Please restore to them immediately their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses, along with the percentage of the money, grain, new wine, and oil that you have been assessing them.” (5:11).

“We will restore it,” they replied, “and will require nothing more from them. We will do as you say.” So I summoned the priests and required of the nobles and officials an oath that they would do what they had promised. (5:12).

I also shook out the folds of my robe and said, “May God likewise shake out of his house and possessions every man who does not keep this promise. May such a man be shaken out and have nothing!” The whole assembly said, “Amen,” and they praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised. (5:13).

Furthermore, from the day King Artaxerxes appointed me to be their governor in the land of Judah, from his twentieth year until his thirty-second year (twelve years total), neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor. (5:14).

The governors before me had heavily burdened the people, taking from them bread and wine plus forty shekels of silver. Their servants also oppressed the people. But I did not do this, because of my fear of God. (5:15).
Instead, I devoted myself to the construction of the wall, and all my servants were gathered there for the work; we did not acquire any land. (5:16).
There were 150 Jews and officials at my table, besides the guests from the surrounding nations. (5:17).

Each day one ox, six choice sheep, and some fowl were prepared for me, and once every ten days an abundance of all kinds of wine was provided. But I did not demand the food allotted to the governor, because the burden on the people was so heavy. (5:18).
Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people. (5:19).
crossRefs: Exodus 22:25-27: Do not act as a creditor or charge interest to the poor, and return a cloak taken in pledge before sundown.
Leviticus 25:35-43: Take no interest from your brother, and an Israelite sold to you serves as a hired worker, not a slave.
Deuteronomy 23:19-20: You shall not charge your brother interest on money, food, or anything that is lent for interest.
Deuteronomy 15:1-11: Every seventh year debts are released, and the hand is to stay open to the poor of the land.
Nehemiah 13:4-13: Nehemiah returns years later to find the same abuses back and the Levites unpaid.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶשֶׁךְ (neshekh, a bite)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word for interest is the word for a bite, the loan taking a piece out of you. The Law bans it outright between Israelites (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20) while allowing it on loans to foreigners. What Nehemiah is confronting in 5:1-5 is not banking; it is neighbours foreclosing on neighbours in a famine.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְאַת הַכֶּסֶף (me'at hakkesef, the hundredth of the money)
translationNotes.note: In 5:11 Nehemiah demands they hand back the fields, vineyards, olive groves and houses, along with 'the hundredth part of the money, grain, new wine and oil' they had been exacting. One percent is normally read as a monthly rate, which comes to twelve percent a year. On a subsistence farm in a bad harvest that is enough to take the land.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּבְשִׁים אֶת־בָּנֵינוּ (kovshim et baneinu, forcing our children into bondage)
translationNotes.note: Debt slavery was legal in Israel and tightly limited: six years of service and release in the seventh (Exodus 21:2), no treatment as a slave, and a return of land at the Jubilee (Leviticus 25:39-43). The complaint in 5:5 is that daughters were already taken and the fathers were powerless because the fields were mortgaged. The king's tax in 5:4 is the pressure behind it, since Persian tribute had to be paid in silver, and a farmer with grain and no silver had to borrow.

translationNotes.term: Shaking out the fold of the robe
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָצְנִי נָעַרְתִּי (chotsni na'arti, I shook out my lap)
translationNotes.note: The chotsen is the fold of the outer garment gathered at the chest, which served as a pocket for carrying grain or coin. Nehemiah shakes his out empty in front of the assembly (5:13) and says God shake out every man who does not keep this promise. It is a curse acted out, and the whole assembly answers Amen.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפֶּחָה (lechem happechah, the bread of the governor)
translationNotes.note: A provincial governor was entitled to a maintenance levy, and Nehemiah says the governors before him took forty shekels of silver a day plus food and wine, and their staff lorded it over the people (5:15). He waived it for the whole twelve years of his term, 445 to 433 BC, while still feeding a table of a hundred and fifty officials plus visitors: one ox, six choice sheep and poultry a day, with a wine resupply every ten days (5:17-18).

stories.keyTakeaway: Nehemiah confronts debt slavery and interest among the nobles and restores justice for the poor.

stories.title: 🛡️ Nehemiah 6
summaryBullets: When Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab, and the rest of our enemies heard that I had rebuilt the wall and not a gap was left— though to that time I had not yet installed the doors in the gates— (6:1).
Sanballat and Geshem sent me this message: “Come, let us meet together in one of the villages on the plain of Ono.” But they were planning to harm me. (6:2).
So I sent messengers to them, saying, “I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?” (6:3).
Four times they sent me the same message, and each time I gave the same reply. (6:4).
The fifth time, Sanballat sent me this same message by his young servant, who had in his hand an unsealed letter (6:5).

that read: “It is reported among the nations— and Geshem agrees— that you and the Jews are plotting to revolt, and this is why you are building the wall. According to these reports, you are to become their king, (6:6).
and you have even appointed prophets in Jerusalem to proclaim on your behalf: ‘There is a king in Judah.’ Soon these rumors will reach the ears of the king. So come, let us confer together.” (6:7).
Then I sent him this reply: “There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind.” (6:8).
For they were all trying to frighten us, saying, “Their hands will be weakened in the work, and it will never be finished.” But now, my God, strengthen my hands. (6:9).

Later, I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah, the son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his house. He said: “Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors because they are coming to kill you — by night they are coming to kill you!” (6:10).
But I replied, “Should a man like me run away? Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life? I will not go!” (6:11).
I realized that God had not sent him, but that he had uttered this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. (6:12).
He had been hired to intimidate me so that I would sin by doing as he suggested, so they could give me a bad name in order to discredit me. (6:13).
O my God, remember Tobiah and Sanballat for what they have done, and also Noadiah the prophetess and the other prophets who tried to intimidate me. (6:14).
So the wall was completed in fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth of Elul. (6:15).
When all our enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened, for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God. (6:16).
Also in those days, the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah’s letters kept coming to them. (6:17).
For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, since he was a son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Jehohanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah. (6:18).
Moreover, these nobles kept reporting to me Tobiah’s good deeds, and they relayed my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me. (6:19).
crossRefs: Ezra 4:11-16: The text of an earlier written accusation to a Persian king, charging that a rebuilt Jerusalem means rebellion.
Numbers 18:7: Anyone not of the priestly line who comes near the holy things is to be put to death.
2 Chronicles 26:16-21: King Uzziah enters the temple to burn incense, is opposed by the priests, and is struck with leprosy.
Deuteronomy 18:20-22: The prophet who speaks a word the LORD has not commanded, and how to tell it did not come from Him.
Micah 3:5-11: Prophets who cry peace when they are fed, and heads who judge for a bribe and priests who teach for hire.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בִּקְעַת אוֹנוֹ (biq'at Ono)
translationNotes.note: Ono lay on the coastal plain near Lod, roughly twenty-five miles northwest of Jerusalem and outside the province of Judah. The invitation in 6:2 is to meet in one of its villages, which means neutral ground, a day's hard travel away, with no Judean force nearby. Nehemiah's answer is that he is doing a great work and cannot come down.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִגֶּרֶת פְּתוּחָה (iggeret petuchah)
translationNotes.note: The fifth message comes unsealed (6:5). A private letter was rolled, tied and sealed with clay or wax so that a broken seal proved tampering; an open one could be read by every courier, official and clerk who handled it on the road. Sending the accusation unsealed was the publication of a rumour, not a communication.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶל־תּוֹךְ הַהֵיכָל (el tokh haheikhal, into the middle of the temple building)
translationNotes.note: Shemaiah urges Nehemiah to shut himself inside the temple building for safety (6:10). Nehemiah was a layman, and Numbers 18:7 makes entry into the sanctuary by anyone outside the priesthood a capital matter; King Uzziah was struck with leprosy for less (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). Taking the advice would have handed his enemies a lawful charge, which is exactly what 6:13 says it was for.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶשְׂרִים וַחֲמִשָּׁה לֶאֱלוּל (esrim va-chamishah le-Elul, the twenty-fifth of Elul)
translationNotes.note: Elul is the sixth month, mid-August to mid-September, the dry end of summer when there is no rain to stop masonry work and no harvest left to bring in. The wall closed on the twenty-fifth of Elul, 445 BC. Fifty-two days is repair and gap-filling on an existing line, not construction from bare rock.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נוֹעַדְיָה הַנְּבִיאָה (No'adyah hannevi'ah, Noadiah the prophetess)
translationNotes.note: Verse 14 names her with 'the rest of the prophets who were trying to make me afraid'. Prophecy could be bought in this period, and the Law had already set the test for it (Deuteronomy 18:20-22), as Micah 3:11 had already named the price. The threat here is not an army; it is religious authority for rent.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בַּעֲלֵי שְׁבוּעָה (ba'alei shevu'ah, men bound by oath)
translationNotes.note: Verses 17-19 report that many nobles of Judah were sworn to Tobiah because he had married the daughter of Shecaniah and his son had married the daughter of Meshullam, both Judean families that appear in the building lists. Letters went back and forth constantly, and men reported Nehemiah's business to him. It is the same insider access that lets Tobiah move into a temple storeroom in 13:4-9.

stories.keyTakeaway: Despite plots, slander, and betrayal, Nehemiah finishes the wall in fifty-two days.

stories.title: 📜 Nehemiah 7
summaryBullets: When the wall had been rebuilt and I had set the doors in place, the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites were appointed. (7:1).
Then I put my brother Hanani in charge of Jerusalem, along with Hananiah the commander of the fortress, because he was a faithful man who feared God more than most. (7:2).

And I told them, “Do not open the gates of Jerusalem until the sun is hot. While the guards are on duty, keep the doors shut and securely fastened. And appoint the residents of Jerusalem as guards, some at their posts and some at their own homes.” (7:3).
Now the city was large and spacious, but there were few people in it, and the houses had not yet been rebuilt. (7:4).

Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles, the officials, and the people to be enrolled by genealogy. I found the genealogical register of those who had first returned, and I found the following written in it: (7:5).

These are the people of the province who came up from the captivity of the exiles carried away to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar its king. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town, (7:6).
accompanied by Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, and Baanah. This is the count of the men of Israel: (7:7).
the descendants of Parosh, 2,172; (7:8).
the descendants of Shephatiah, 372; (7:9).
the descendants of Arah, 652; (7:10).
the descendants of Pahath-moab (through the line of Jeshua and Joab), 2,818; (7:11).
the descendants of Elam, 1,254; (7:12).
the descendants of Zattu, 845; (7:13).
the descendants of Zaccai, 760; (7:14).
the descendants of Binnui, 648; (7:15).
the descendants of Bebai, 628; (7:16).
the descendants of Azgad, 2,322; (7:17).
the descendants of Adonikam, 667; (7:18).
the descendants of Bigvai, 2,067; (7:19).
the descendants of Adin, 655; (7:20).
the descendants of Ater (through Hezekiah), 98; (7:21).
the descendants of Hashum, 328; (7:22).
the descendants of Bezai, 324; (7:23).
the descendants of Hariph, 112; (7:24).
the descendants of Gibeon, 95; (7:25).
the men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188; (7:26).
the men of Anathoth, 128; (7:27).
the men of Beth-azmaveth, 42; (7:28).
the men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743; (7:29).
the men of Ramah and Geba, 621; (7:30).
the men of Michmash, 122; (7:31).
the men of Bethel and Ai, 123; (7:32).
the men of the other Nebo, 52; (7:33).
the descendants of the other Elam, 1,254; (7:34).
the descendants of Harim, 320; (7:35).
the men of Jericho, 345; (7:36).
the men of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 721; (7:37).
and the descendants of Senaah, 3,930. (7:38).
The priests: the descendants of Jedaiah (through the house of Jeshua), 973; (7:39).
the descendants of Immer, 1,052; (7:40).
the descendants of Pashhur, 1,247; (7:41).
and the descendants of Harim, 1,017. (7:42).
The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua (through Kadmiel, through the line of Hodevah), 74. (7:43).
The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 148. (7:44).

The gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, the descendants of Ater, the descendants of Talmon, the descendants of Akkub, the descendants of Hatita, and the descendants of Shobai, 138 in all. (7:45).
The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, the descendants of Hasupha, the descendants of Tabbaoth, (7:46).
the descendants of Keros, the descendants of Sia, the descendants of Padon, (7:47).
the descendants of Lebanah, the descendants of Hagabah, the descendants of Shalmai, (7:48).
the descendants of Hanan, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Gahar, (7:49).
the descendants of Reaiah, the descendants of Rezin, the descendants of Nekoda, (7:50).
the descendants of Gazzam, the descendants of Uzza, the descendants of Paseah, (7:51).
the descendants of Besai, the descendants of Meunim, the descendants of Nephushesim, (7:52).
the descendants of Bakbuk, the descendants of Hakupha, the descendants of Harhur, (7:53).
the descendants of Bazlith, the descendants of Mehida, the descendants of Harsha, (7:54).
the descendants of Barkos, the descendants of Sisera, the descendants of Temah, (7:55).
the descendants of Neziah, and the descendants of Hatipha. (7:56).
The descendants of the servants of Solomon: the descendants of Sotai, the descendants of Sophereth, the descendants of Perida, (7:57).
the descendants of Jaala, the descendants of Darkon, the descendants of Giddel, (7:58).
the descendants of Shephatiah, the descendants of Hattil, the descendants of Pochereth-hazzebaim, and the descendants of Amon. (7:59).
The temple servants and descendants of the servants of Solomon numbered 392 in all. (7:60).
The following came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not prove that their families were descended from Israel: (7:61).
the descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah, and the descendants of Nekoda, 642 in all. (7:62).

And from among the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz, and the descendants of Barzillai (who had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name). (7:63).
These men searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. (7:64).
The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim. (7:65).
The whole assembly numbered 42,360, (7:66).
in addition to their 7,337 menservants and maidservants, as well as their 245 male and female singers. (7:67).
They had 736 horses, 245 mules, (7:68).
435 camels, and 6,720 donkeys. (7:69).
Some of the heads of the families contributed to the project. The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 darics of gold, 50 bowls, and 530 priestly garments. (7:70).
And some of the heads of the families gave to the treasury for the project 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver. (7:71).
The rest of the people gave a total of 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 priestly garments. (7:72).

So the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, and temple servants, along with some of the people and the rest of the Israelites, settled in their own towns. And by the seventh month the Israelites had settled in their towns. (7:73).
crossRefs: Ezra 2:1-70: The same register of families who came back with Zerubbabel, copied from the earlier record.
1 Chronicles 9:17-27: The gatekeepers, their four sides, their night watches and their charge of the keys.
Numbers 1:1-19: Israel counted clan by clan and household by household, with a named man for each tribe.
Nehemiah 11:1-2: The lot that moves one family in ten into the empty city this census exposes.
Psalm 87:5-6: The LORD records the peoples in a register, noting who was born in Zion.

translationNotes.term: The gates opened late and barred early
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַד־חֹם הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ (ad chom hashemesh, until the sun is hot)
translationNotes.note: City gates normally opened at first light so farmers and traders could get moving. Nehemiah orders them kept shut until the sun is hot and barred again while the gatekeepers are still on duty (7:3), with residents standing watch opposite their own houses. A wall is only as good as its gate discipline, and this is a garrison order, not a routine.

translationNotes.term: A large city with almost nobody in it
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְהָעָם מְעַט בְּתוֹכָהּ (veha-am me'at betokhah, and the people in it were few)
translationNotes.note: Verse 4 states the problem the census is meant to measure: the city was wide and large, the people inside it few, and the houses not yet rebuilt. Judah's population was living in the villages where the fields were. That is why chapter 11 has to draft settlers by lot.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְהִתְיַחֵשׂ (lehityaches, to be enrolled by descent)
translationNotes.note: Nehemiah says he found the book of the genealogy of those who came up first, and copied it (7:5). Descent decided who could serve at the altar and who held a claim on a family plot of land. Verses 61-65 record the families who could not produce their papers, and the priests among them were suspended from the holy food until a priest should arise with Urim and Thummim.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דַּרְכְּמוֹן (darkemon, daric) - מָנֶה (maneh, mina)
translationNotes.note: The building fund is itemised in 7:70-72: the governor gives 1,000 gold darics, 50 basins and 530 priests' garments; the heads of families give 20,000 darics and 2,200 minas of silver; the rest of the people 20,000 darics, 2,000 minas and 67 garments. A daric held about 8.4 grams of gold, so the 41,000 darics come to roughly 344 kilograms, about 760 pounds, of gold. A mina of silver ran a little over a pound.

translationNotes.term: Temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְתִינִים (netinim, the given ones)
translationNotes.note: Two hereditary classes of temple labour, listed by family in 7:46-60 after the singers and gatekeepers, three hundred and ninety-two men in total. Their work was the physical support of the sanctuary: water, wood, hauling and cleaning. Joshua 9:23-27 puts the Gibeonites under exactly that obligation for the altar of the LORD.

stories.keyTakeaway: After the doors are set in place, Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers, singers, and Levites, charges Hanani and Hananiah with guarding the spacious but sparsely settled city, and finds the genealogical register of those who first returned with Zerubbabel; it lists the families, priests, Levites, and temple servants, including priests barred from the most holy things for lack of family records until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim.

stories.title: 📖 Nehemiah 8
summaryBullets: At that time all the people gathered together in the square before the Water Gate, and they asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded for Israel. (8:1).
On the first day of the seventh month, Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly of men and women and all who could listen and understand. (8:2).

So Ezra read it aloud from daybreak until noon as he faced the square before the Water Gate, in front of the men and women and those who could understand. And all the people listened attentively to the Book of the Law. (8:3).

Ezra the scribe stood on a high wooden platform built for this occasion. At his right side stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, and at his left were Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hash-baddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam. (8:4).
Ezra opened the book in full view of all the people, since he was standing above them all, and as he opened it, all the people stood up. (8:5).
Then Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and with their hands uplifted, all the people said, “Amen, Amen!” Then they bowed down and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground. (8:6).

The Levites — Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, and Pelaiah — instructed the people in the Law as they stood in their places. (8:7).
So they read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read. (8:8).

Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were instructing the people said to all of them, “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.” For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law. (8:9).

Then Nehemiah told them, “Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” (8:10).
And the Levites calmed all the people, saying, “Be still, since today is holy. Do not grieve.” (8:11).
Then all the people began to eat and drink, to send out portions, and to rejoice greatly, because they understood the words that had been made known to them. (8:12).
On the second day of the month, the heads of all the families, along with the priests and Levites, gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law. (8:13).
And they found written in the Law, which the LORD had commanded through Moses, that the Israelites were to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month, (8:14).

and that they should proclaim this message and spread it throughout their towns and in Jerusalem, saying, “Go out to the hill country and bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees, to make booths, as it is written.” (8:15).

And the people went out, brought back branches, and made booths on their own rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and by the Gate of Ephraim. (8:16).

The whole assembly that had returned from exile made booths and lived in them. From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this. And there was great rejoicing. (8:17).

Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God. The Israelites kept the feast for seven days, and on the eighth day they held an assembly, according to the ordinance. (8:18).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 31:9-13: Moses commands that the Law be read to all Israel, men, women and children, every seventh year at the Feast of Booths.
Leviticus 23:33-43: The Feast of Booths, its branches, and the command to live in shelters seven days as a memorial of the exodus.
2 Kings 23:1-3: Josiah reads the whole book of the covenant aloud to the people and they stand to it.
Ezra 7:6-10: Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to do it, and to teach its statutes in Israel.
Nehemiah 9:1-3: Two weeks later the same assembly reads for a quarter of the day and confesses for another quarter.

translationNotes.term: The square before the Water Gate
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָרְחוֹב אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי שַׁעַר־הַמָּיִם (harechov asher lifnei sha'ar hammayim)
translationNotes.note: An open plaza inside the east wall, near the Gihon spring that gave the gate its name. The reading runs from first light until midday (8:3), roughly six hours, with the people standing. They asked for it themselves: 8:1 says the people told Ezra to bring the book.

translationNotes.term: A wooden platform built for the purpose
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִגְדַּל־עֵץ (migdal ets, tower of wood)
translationNotes.note: Verse 4 says they made a tower of wood for the reading and names thirteen men who stood on it with Ezra, six at his right hand and seven at his left. It was built for this one occasion so the reader could be seen and heard by a standing crowd. Every name is recorded, which is how the assembly certified who was present.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְפֹרָשׁ וְשׂוֹם שֶׂכֶל (meforash ve-som sekhel, made distinct and giving the sense)
translationNotes.note: The Levites are named in 8:7-8 as going through the assembly explaining while Ezra read. The Law was in Hebrew; after generations in Babylon and under Persian administration, Aramaic was the common tongue, which is why whole sections of Ezra and Daniel are written in it. Verse 8 is the earliest description in Scripture of Scripture being read aloud and explained so that ordinary people understood it.

translationNotes.term: Send portions to those who have nothing
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָנוֹת (manot, portions)
translationNotes.note: When the people weep at what they hear, they are told to eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to anyone with nothing prepared (8:10, 12). Sending manot was the standing form of festival charity: you did not invite the poor to your table, you carried food to their house. The same custom is written into the law of Purim in Esther 9:19-22.

translationNotes.term: Booths of branches on the roofs
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֻכּוֹת (sukkot, shelters)
translationNotes.note: They go to the hills for olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm and leafy branches and build shelters on their flat roofs, in their courtyards, in the temple courts and in the two public squares (8:15-16). Leviticus 23:40 is the command they are reading. Verse 17 records that it had not been kept like this since the days of Joshua son of Nun.

translationNotes.term: The Book of the Law of Moses
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר תּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה (sefer torat Mosheh)
translationNotes.note: A scroll, not a codex: sheets of prepared skin sewn end to end and rolled on two staves, read by unrolling with one hand and rolling with the other. When Ezra opens it in the sight of all the people, they can see him do it, which is why 8:5 says they all stood up at that moment.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ezra reads the Law publicly, the Levites explain it, and the people celebrate the Feast of Booths with great joy.

stories.title: ✍️ Nehemiah 9
summaryBullets: On the twenty-fourth day of the same month, the Israelites gathered together, fasting and wearing sackcloth, with dust on their heads. (9:1).
Those of Israelite descent separated themselves from all the foreigners, and they stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. (9:2).

While they stood in their places, they read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day, and they spent another quarter of the day in confession and worship of the LORD their God. (9:3).
And the Levites — Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani — stood on the raised platform and cried out in a loud voice to the LORD their God. (9:4).

Then the Levites— Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah— said, “Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting: Blessed be Your glorious name, and may it be exalted above all blessing and praise. (9:5).

You alone are the LORD. You created the heavens, the highest heavens with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them. You give life to all things, and the host of heaven worships You. (9:6).
You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram, who brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham. (9:7).

You found his heart faithful before You, and made a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites and Hittites, of the Amorites and Perizzites, of the Jebusites and Girgashites— to give it to his descendants. You have kept Your promise, because You are righteous. (9:8).
You saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt; You heard their cry at the Red Sea. (9:9).

You performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh, all his officials, and all the people of his land, for You knew they had acted with arrogance against our fathers. You made a name for Yourself that endures to this day. (9:10).
You divided the sea before them, and they crossed through it on dry ground. You hurled their pursuers into the depths like a stone into raging waters. (9:11).
You led them with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way in which they should travel. (9:12).
You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven. You gave them just ordinances, true laws, and good statutes and commandments. (9:13).
You revealed to them Your holy Sabbath and gave them commandments and statutes and laws through Your servant Moses. (9:14).
In their hunger You gave them bread from heaven; in their thirst You brought them water from the rock. You told them to go in and possess the land that You had sworn to give them. (9:15).
But they and our fathers became arrogant and stiff-necked and did not obey Your commandments. (9:16).

They refused to listen and failed to remember the wonders You performed among them. They stiffened their necks and appointed a leader to return them to their bondage in Egypt. But You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion, and You did not forsake them. (9:17).
Even when they cast for themselves an image of a calf and said, ‘This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,’ and when they committed terrible blasphemies, (9:18).

You in Your great compassion did not forsake them in the wilderness. By day the pillar of cloud never turned away from guiding them on their path; and by the night the pillar of fire illuminated the way they should go. (9:19).
You gave Your good Spirit to instruct them. You did not withhold Your manna from their mouths, and You gave them water for their thirst. (9:20).
For forty years You sustained them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell. (9:21).
You gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted to them every corner of the land. So they took the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and of Og king of Bashan. (9:22).
You multiplied their descendants like the stars of heaven and brought them to the land You had told their fathers to enter and possess. (9:23).

So their descendants went in and possessed the land; You subdued before them the Canaanites dwelling in the land. You delivered into their hands the kings and peoples of the land, to do with them as they wished. (9:24).

They captured fortified cities and fertile land and took houses full of all goods, wells already dug, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees in abundance. So they ate and were filled; they grew fat and delighted in Your great goodness. (9:25).

But they were disobedient and rebelled against You; they flung Your law behind their backs. They killed Your prophets, who had admonished them to return to You. They committed terrible blasphemies. (9:26).

So You delivered them into the hands of enemies who oppressed them, and in their time of distress they cried out to You. From heaven You heard them, and in Your great compassion You gave them deliverers who saved them from the hands of their enemies. (9:27).

But as soon as they had rest, they again did evil in Your sight. So You abandoned them to the hands of their enemies, who had dominion over them. When they cried out to You again, You heard from heaven, and You delivered them many times in Your compassion. (9:28).

You admonished them to turn back to Your law, but they were arrogant and disobeyed Your commandments. They sinned against Your ordinances, by which a man will live if he practices them. They turned a stubborn shoulder; they stiffened their necks and would not obey. (9:29).
You were patient with them for many years, and Your Spirit admonished them through Your prophets. Yet they would not listen, so You gave them into the hands of the neighboring peoples. (9:30).
But in Your great compassion, You did not put an end to them; nor did You forsake them, for You are a gracious and compassionate God. (9:31).

So now, our God, the great and mighty and awesome God who keeps His gracious covenant, do not view lightly all the hardship that has come upon us, and upon our kings and leaders, our priests and prophets, our ancestors and all Your people, from the days of the kings of Assyria until today. (9:32).
You are just in all that has befallen us, because You have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly. (9:33).
Our kings and leaders and priests and fathers did not obey Your law or listen to Your commandments and warnings that You gave them. (9:34).

For even while they were in their kingdom, with the abundant goodness that You had given them, and in the spacious and fertile land that You had set before them, they would not serve You or turn from their wicked ways. (9:35).
So here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy its fruit and goodness— here we are as slaves! (9:36).
Its abundant harvest goes to the kings You have set over us because of our sins. And they rule over our bodies and our livestock as they please. We are in great distress. (9:37).
In view of all this, we make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it with the names of our leaders, Levites, and priests.” (9:38).
crossRefs: Genesis 15:7-21: The LORD brings Abram out of Ur of the Chaldeans and cuts a covenant with him over the land.
Exodus 13:21-22: The pillar of cloud by day and fire by night that never left the people, cited in this prayer.
Deuteronomy 8:2-4: Forty years in the wilderness where their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell.
Judges 2:11-19: The repeating pattern the prayer summarises: they did evil, He gave them to enemies, they cried out, He raised judges.
Psalm 106:6-46: The same national history prayed as confession, from Egypt to the exile.

translationNotes.term: Sackcloth and earth on their heads
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּשַׂקִּים וַאֲדָמָה עֲלֵיהֶם (be-saqqim va-adamah aleihem)
translationNotes.note: Sackcloth is coarse dark goat-hair cloth worn against the skin, uncomfortable on purpose, the standard dress of grief and repentance (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5). Putting dirt on the head goes with it (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12). The assembly in 9:1 does both, two days after the week of Booths ended, so a festival of joy is followed straight away by a day of mourning.

translationNotes.term: A quarter of the day reading, a quarter confessing
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְבִעִית הַיּוֹם (revi'it hayyom, a fourth of the day)
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 divides a daylight day of about twelve hours into shares: some three hours standing while the Law was read, and another three confessing and worshipping. The prayer that follows in 9:5-37 is one of the longest in Scripture and covers creation, Abraham, the exodus, Sinai, the wilderness, the land, the judges, the prophets and the exile in order.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים (Ur Kasdim)
translationNotes.note: A major Sumerian city in southern Mesopotamia near the lower Euphrates, in what is now southern Iraq, excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s and 1930s. It was a walled city with a great ziggurat to the moon god, not a village. The prayer starts Israel's story with God bringing one man out of an established pagan metropolis (9:7; Genesis 15:7).

translationNotes.term: You are the LORD, You alone
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַתָּה־הוּא יְהוָה לְבַדֶּךָ (attah hu YHWH levaddekha)
translationNotes.note: The prayer opens by naming God as maker of heaven, the highest heavens, all their host, the earth and the seas (9:6), then moves straight to Abram. It is a confession built as a history lesson, and every claim in it is taken from books the assembly had just heard read aloud.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲמָנָה (amanah, a binding agreement)
translationNotes.note: Verse 38 closes the confession with a signed document rather than a feeling: they make a firm agreement in writing, and the princes, Levites and priests set their seals on it. Amanah comes from the root behind the word amen, meaning what is firm and reliable. The list of who sealed it opens the next chapter.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲבָדִים אֲנַחְנוּ הַיּוֹם (avadim anachnu hayyom)
translationNotes.note: Verses 36-37 state their political situation without decoration: they are in the land, but its rich yield goes to the kings Persia has set over them, and those kings rule over their bodies and their cattle as they please. Judah in 445 BC is a taxed province, not a kingdom. That is the condition the covenant of chapter 10 is signed under.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Israelites gather in fasting and sackcloth to confess their sins and those of their ancestors; Levites lead them in reading the Law and in a lengthy prayer recounting God's faithfulness from Abraham through the wilderness and settlement, contrasted with Israel's repeated disobedience, before concluding that their present slavery results from their own wickedness.

“The rest of the people— the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and all who had separated themselves from the people of the land to obey the Law of God— along with their wives and all their sons and daughters who are able to understand, (10:28).

hereby join with their noble brothers and commit themselves with a sworn oath to follow the Law of God given through His servant Moses and to obey carefully all the commandments, ordinances, and statutes of the LORD our Lord. (10:29).
We will not give our daughters in marriage to the people of the land, and we will not take their daughters for our sons. (10:30).

When the people of the land bring merchandise or any kind of grain to sell on the Sabbath day, we will not buy from them on a Sabbath or holy day. Every seventh year we will let the fields lie fallow and will cancel every debt. (10:31).
We also place ourselves under the obligation to contribute a third of a shekel yearly for the service of the house of our God: (10:32).

for the showbread, for the regular grain offerings and burnt offerings, for the Sabbath offerings, for the New Moons and appointed feasts, for the holy offerings, for the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the duties of the house of our God. (10:33).

We have cast lots among the priests, Levites, and people for the donation of wood by our families at the appointed times each year. They are to bring it to the house of our God to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law. (10:34).
We will also bring the firstfruits of our land and of every fruit tree to the house of the LORD year by year. (10:35).

And we will bring the firstborn of our sons and our livestock, as it is written in the Law, and will bring the firstborn of our herds and flocks to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God. (10:36).

Moreover, we will bring to the priests at the storerooms of the house of our God the firstfruits of our dough, of our grain offerings, of the fruit of all our trees, and of our new wine and oil. A tenth of our produce belongs to the Levites, so that they shall receive tithes in all the towns where we labor. (10:37).

A priest of Aaron’s line is to accompany the Levites when they collect the tenth, and the Levites are to bring a tenth of these tithes to the storerooms of the treasury in the house of our God. (10:38).

For the Israelites and the Levites are to bring the contributions of grain, new wine, and oil to the storerooms where the articles of the sanctuary are kept and where the ministering priests, the gatekeepers, and the singers stay. Thus we will not neglect the house of our God.” (10:39).
crossRefs: Exodus 30:11-16: Every man counted pays half a shekel for the service of the tent of meeting, rich and poor alike.
Leviticus 25:1-7: The land keeps a sabbath to the LORD in the seventh year; you shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard.
Numbers 18:21-32: The tithe belongs to the Levites for their service, and they in turn give a tithe of the tithe to the priests.
Deuteronomy 26:1-11: Firstfruits carried in a basket to the place the LORD chooses, with the words the giver must say.
Leviticus 6:12-13: The fire on the altar must be kept burning; the priest lays wood on it every morning and it must never go out.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַחֲתוּמִים (hachatumim, the sealed ones)
translationNotes.note: Eighty-four names head the covenant, starting with Nehemiah the governor: priests, Levites, then heads of families. A seal was a carved stone or ring pressed into wet clay attached to a rolled and tied document, and hundreds of such clay sealings from Judah have been found. The seal was the signature, and a broken one meant the document had been opened.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁלִשִׁית הַשֶּׁקֶל (shelishit hasheqel)
translationNotes.note: They bind themselves to a yearly charge of a third of a shekel for the service of the house (10:32): the showbread, the daily grain offering and burnt offering, the sabbaths, new moons, festivals and the sin offerings. The census levy of Exodus 30:13 was half a shekel. The text says plainly they laid this obligation on themselves, and a third of a shekel is what a poor province could actually raise.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֻרְבַּן הָעֵצִים (qorban ha-etsim, the offering of wood)
translationNotes.note: The altar fire had to burn continuously (Leviticus 6:12-13), which takes a steady supply of cut wood in a country with little forest. Verse 34 has priests, Levites and people cast lots to fix which family delivers wood at which season each year. Josephus records that the day of wood carrying was still kept as a fixed occasion in the temple's last decades (Jewish War 2.425).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּכוֹר בָּנֵינוּ (bekhor baneinu, the firstborn of our sons)
translationNotes.note: Verses 35-37 gather the whole schedule of dues: firstfruits of the ground and of every tree, the firstborn of sons and of herds and flocks, the first of the dough, the grain, wine and oil. A firstborn son was not offered but bought back for five shekels of silver paid to the priests (Numbers 18:15-16). The firstborn of clean animals went to the altar.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲשַׂר הַמַּעֲשֵׂר (ma'asar hamma'aser)
translationNotes.note: Levites collected the tithe in the farming towns, and a priest of Aaron's line had to be present when they did it (10:38); the Levites then brought a tenth of what they received up to the temple storerooms. Numbers 18:26 is the rule. The whole system ran on grain and oil moving physically into chambers in the temple, which is why chapter 13 opens with a fight over one of those rooms.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁבָּת (shabbat)
translationNotes.note: The clause in 10:31 covers two rests: no buying from the peoples of the land who bring goods to sell on the sabbath or a holy day, and forgoing the crops of the seventh year along with every debt. The seventh day rest is commanded in Exodus 20:8-11; the seventh year rest for the land in Leviticus 25:1-7 and the release of debts in Deuteronomy 15:1-2. The market pressure was real, and 13:15-22 shows the clause breaking down.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nehemiah, priests, Levites, and leaders of the people sign a binding agreement to keep God's Law, including prohibitions on intermarriage with foreigners and Sabbath commerce, and commitments to support the temple with annual contributions and offerings.

stories.title: 🏘️ Nehemiah 11

And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem. (11:2).

These are the heads of the provinces who settled in Jerusalem. (In the villages of Judah, however, each lived on his own property in their towns— the Israelites, priests, Levites, temple servants, and descendants of Solomon’s servants— (11:3).

while some of the descendants of Judah and Benjamin settled in Jerusalem.) From the descendants of Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah, the son of Zechariah, the son of Amariah, the son of Shephatiah, the son of Mahalalel, a descendant of Perez; (11:4).
and Maaseiah son of Baruch, the son of Col-hozeh, the son of Hazaiah, the son of Adaiah, the son of Joiarib, the son of Zechariah, a descendant of Shelah. (11:5).
