crossRefs: Nehemiah 7:4-5: The city was wide and large, the people in it few, and the houses not yet rebuilt.
1 Chronicles 9:2-16: The first to resettle on their own property in the towns, and the priests and Levites who lived in Jerusalem.
Joshua 18:8-10: Joshua casts lots before the LORD at Shiloh to assign the land among the tribes.
Proverbs 16:33: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.
1 Chronicles 23:28-32: The Levites' assigned charge of the courts, the chambers, the showbread and the measures.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶחָד מִן־הָעֲשָׂרָה (echad min ha-asarah)
translationNotes.note: Living in Jerusalem was a cost, not a prize. The fields, olive groves and family plots were in the villages, and the city was the place an enemy would strike first. So the leaders lived there and one household in ten was drafted by lot, while 11:2 records that the people blessed the men who volunteered on top of the draft.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָעֹפֶל (ha-Ofel, the swelling)
translationNotes.note: The name means a bulge or rise, and it is the slope between the old City of David and the temple platform on the eastern ridge. The temple servants lived there (11:21), close to the work. Nehemiah 3:26-27 has the wall repaired along it, and 2 Chronicles 27:3 credits Jotham with building there.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁעֲרִים (sho'arim)
translationNotes.note: A hereditary Levitical office, a hundred and seventy-two men at the gates by this count (11:19). The job was not doorman: they controlled access to the temple courts, held the keys, kept night watches on all four sides and had charge of the chambers and stores (1 Chronicles 9:17-27). They opened the house every morning.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲמָנָה עַל־הַמְשֹׁרְרִים (amanah al hamshorerim, a settled agreement about the singers)
translationNotes.note: Verses 22-23 note that the singers were under a royal order with a fixed daily allowance. Temple music was full-time work, so the men doing it had to be provisioned rather than farming. Their overseer is named as Uzzi, of the sons of Asaph, the guild David set over the song (1 Chronicles 25:1-2).

translationNotes.term: The towns from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִבְּאֵר־שֶׁבַע עַד־גֵּיא־הִנֹּם (mi-Be'er Sheva ad Gei Hinnom)
translationNotes.note: The settlement list in 11:25-36 runs south to Beersheba, about forty-five miles from Jerusalem at the edge of the Negev desert, and west to Lachish and Azekah in the Shephelah foothills, with the men of Benjamin north of the city. The Persian province of Yehud that Nehemiah governed was a fraction of that, a strip of hill country around Jerusalem. The list records where Judah and Benjamin actually lived, which reached well past the province line.

stories.keyTakeaway: Leaders and people are assigned to live in Jerusalem through a lottery system; the chapter lists the settlers by tribe, including priests, Levites, gatekeepers, and temple servants, along with the towns where others remained.

stories.title: 🎶 Nehemiah 12
summaryBullets: Now these are the priests and Levites who went up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and with Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra, (12:1).
Amariah, Malluch, Hattush, (12:2).
Shecaniah, Rehum, Meremoth, (12:3).
Iddo, Ginnethon, Abijah, (12:4).
Mijamin, Maadiah, Bilgah, (12:5).
Shemaiah, Joiarib, Jedaiah, (12:6).
Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the leaders of the priests and their associates in the days of Jeshua. (12:7).
The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, who, with his associates, led the songs of thanksgiving. (12:8).
Bakbukiah and Unni, their associates, stood across from them in the services. (12:9).
Jeshua was the father of Joiakim, Joiakim was the father of Eliashib, Eliashib was the father of Joiada, (12:10).
Joiada was the father of Jonathan, and Jonathan was the father of Jaddua. (12:11).
In the days of Joiakim, these were the heads of the priestly families: of the family of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah; (12:12).
of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan; (12:13).
of Malluchi, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph; (12:14).
of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai; (12:15).
of Iddo, Zechariah; of Ginnethon, Meshullam; (12:16).
of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin and of Moadiah, Piltai; (12:17).
of Bilgah, Shammua; of Shemaiah, Jonathan; (12:18).
of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi; (12:19).
of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber; (12:20).
of Hilkiah, Hashabiah; and of Jedaiah, Nethanel. (12:21).
In the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua, during the reign of Darius the Persian, the heads of the families of the Levites and priests were recorded. (12:22).
As for the descendants of Levi, the family heads up to the days of Johanan son of Eliashib were recorded in the Book of the Chronicles. (12:23).

The leaders of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua son of Kadmiel, along with their associates, who stood across from them to give praise and thanksgiving as one section alternated with the other, as prescribed by David the man of God. (12:24).
Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were gatekeepers who guarded the storerooms at the gates. (12:25).
They served in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe. (12:26).

At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, the Levites were sought out from all their homes and brought to Jerusalem to celebrate the joyous dedication with thanksgiving and singing, accompanied by cymbals, harps, and lyres. (12:27).
The singers were also assembled from the region around Jerusalem, from the villages of the Netophathites, (12:28).
from Beth-gilgal, and from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, for they had built villages for themselves around Jerusalem. (12:29).
After the priests and Levites had purified themselves, they purified the people, the gates, and the wall. (12:30).
Then I brought the leaders of Judah up on the wall, and I appointed two great thanksgiving choirs. One was to proceed along the top of the wall to the right, toward the Dung Gate. (12:31).
Hoshaiah and half the leaders of Judah followed, (12:32).
along with Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam, (12:33).
Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, Jeremiah, (12:34).
and some of the priests with trumpets, and also Zechariah son of Jonathan, the son of Shemaiah, the son of Mattaniah, the son of Micaiah, the son of Zaccur, the son of Asaph, (12:35).

and his associates— Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani— with the musical instruments prescribed by David the man of God. Ezra the scribe led the procession. (12:36).
At the Fountain Gate they went directly up the steps of the City of David on the ascent to the wall and passed above the house of David to the Water Gate on the east. (12:37).
The second thanksgiving choir proceeded to the left, and I followed it with half the people along the top of the wall, past the Tower of the Ovens to the Broad Wall, (12:38).
over the Gate of Ephraim, the Jeshanah Gate, the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel, and the Tower of the Hundred, as far as the Sheep Gate. And they stopped at the Gate of the Guard. (12:39).
The two thanksgiving choirs then stood in the house of God, as did I, along with the half of the officials accompanying me, (12:40).
as well as the priests with their trumpets — Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah — (12:41).
and also Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. Then the choirs sang out under the direction of Jezrahiah. (12:42).
On that day they offered great sacrifices, rejoicing because God had given them great joy. The women and children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar. (12:43).

And on that same day men were appointed over the rooms that housed the supplies, contributions, firstfruits, and tithes. The portions specified by the Law for the priests and Levites were gathered into these storerooms from the fields of the villages, because Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who were serving. (12:44).
They performed the service of their God and the service of purification, along with the singers and gatekeepers, as David and his son Solomon had prescribed. (12:45).
For long ago, in the days of David and Asaph, there were directors for the singers and for the songs of praise and thanksgiving to God. (12:46).

So in the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel contributed the daily portions for the singers and gatekeepers. They also set aside daily portions for the Levites, and the Levites set aside daily portions for the descendants of Aaron. (12:47).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 25:1-8: David sets apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to prophesy with lyres, harps and cymbals.
2 Chronicles 5:11-14: Trumpeters and singers make one sound at the dedication of Solomon's temple, and the glory fills the house.
1 Kings 8:62-66: Solomon and all Israel offer the dedication sacrifices and hold the feast before the LORD.
Ezra 3:10-11: Priests with trumpets and Levites with cymbals sing responsively when the second temple's foundation is laid.
Nehemiah 6:15-16: The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the surrounding nations lose their confidence.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲנֻכָּה (chanukkah)
translationNotes.note: The word simply means dedication or inauguration, the formal handing over of a building for its use. The same noun later names the winter festival marking the rededication of the temple altar, which John 10:22 calls the Feast of Dedication and which Jews keep as Hanukkah. Here it is a wall, not an altar, being dedicated.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁתֵּי תוֹדֹת גְּדוֹלֹת (shetei todot gedolot, two great thanksgiving choirs)
translationNotes.note: They climb onto the finished wall and split, one procession going right past the Dung Gate and the Fountain Gate, the other left past the Tower of the Ovens and the Broad Wall, and they meet at the temple (12:31-40). It is a physical inspection turned into a service: the whole circuit gets walked, in public, by the people who built it. Nehemiah walks with the second group.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְצִלְתַּיִם נְבָלִים וְכִנֹּרוֹת (metsiltayim, nevalim ve-khinnorot, cymbals, harps and lyres) - חֲצֹצְרוֹת (chatsotserot, trumpets)
translationNotes.note: The Levites bring cymbals, harps and lyres, the set David assigned to the singers, and the priests carry the straight silver trumpets of Numbers 10:1-10, which only priests sounded. Verse 36 says the instruments were 'the musical instruments of David the man of God', meaning the pattern of temple music was itself an inherited ordinance.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְשָׁכוֹת (neshakhot, chambers)
translationNotes.note: Verse 44 appoints named men over the chambers that held the contributions, firstfruits and tithes gathered from the fields of each town. These were rooms built into the temple courts, the treasury and pantry of the whole system that chapter 10 had just committed to funding. Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who served, says 12:44, because for the moment they were actually being paid.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּרְיָוֶשׁ הַפָּרְסִי (Daryavesh haParsi)
translationNotes.note: The priestly register in 12:22 is said to run down to the reign of Darius the Persian. Three Persian kings bore the name: Darius I (522-486 BC), Darius II (423-404 BC) and Darius III (336-330 BC), the last of whom Alexander overthrew. The note tells you these lists were kept up as living records after Nehemiah's own lifetime.

stories.keyTakeaway: A roster of priests and Levites returned with Zerubbabel and Joshua, with their family lines recorded through subsequent generations. Nehemiah organizes two choirs to process on the completed wall during a dedication ceremony with music and sacrifices, and afterward appoints officials to collect contributions and tithes for the priests and Levites.

headings.text: The Priests and Levites Who Returned

stories.title: 🔥 Nehemiah 13
summaryBullets: At that time the Book of Moses was read aloud in the hearing of the people, and in it they found the passage stating that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God, (13:1).
because they had not met the Israelites with food and water, but had hired Balaam to call down a curse against them (although our God had turned the curse into a blessing). (13:2).
As soon as the people heard this law, they excluded from Israel all of foreign descent. (13:3).
Now before this, Eliashib the priest, a relative of Tobiah, had been put in charge of the storerooms of the house of our God (13:4).

and had prepared for Tobiah a large room where they had previously stored the grain offerings, the frankincense, the temple articles, and the tithes of grain, new wine, and oil prescribed for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, along with the contributions for the priests. (13:5).

While all this was happening, I was not in Jerusalem, because I had returned to Artaxerxes king of Babylon in the thirty-second year of his reign. Some time later I obtained leave from the king (13:6).
to return to Jerusalem. Then I discovered the evil that Eliashib had done on behalf of Tobiah by providing him a room in the courts of the house of God. (13:7).
And I was greatly displeased and threw all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room. (13:8).
Then I ordered that the rooms be purified, and I had the articles of the house of God restored to them, along with the grain offerings and frankincense. (13:9).
I also learned that because the portions for the Levites had not been given to them, all the Levites and singers responsible for performing the service had gone back to their own fields. (13:10).
So I rebuked the officials and asked, “Why has the house of God been neglected?” Then I gathered the Levites and singers together and stationed them at their posts, (13:11).
and all Judah brought a tenth of the grain, new wine, and oil into the storerooms. (13:12).

I appointed as treasurers over the storerooms Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah of the Levites, with Hanan son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah, to assist them, because they were considered trustworthy. They were responsible for distributing the supplies to their fellow Levites. (13:13).
Remember me for this, O my God, and do not blot out my deeds of loving devotion for the house of my God and for its services. (13:14).

In those days I saw people in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath and bringing in grain and loading it on donkeys, along with wine, grapes, and figs. All kinds of goods were being brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. So I warned them against selling food on that day. (13:15).
Additionally, men of Tyre who lived there were importing fish and all kinds of merchandise and selling them on the Sabbath to the people of Judah in Jerusalem. (13:16).
Then I rebuked the nobles of Judah and asked, “What is this evil you are doing— profaning the Sabbath day? (13:17).
Did not your forefathers do the same things, so that our God brought all this disaster on us and on this city? And now you are rekindling His wrath against Israel by profaning the Sabbath!” (13:18).

When the evening shadows began to fall on the gates of Jerusalem, just before the Sabbath, I ordered that the gates be shut and not opened until after the Sabbath. I posted some of my servants at the gates so that no load could enter on the Sabbath day. (13:19).
Once or twice, the merchants and those who sell all kinds of goods camped outside Jerusalem, (13:20).
but I warned them, “Why are you camping in front of the wall? If you do it again, I will lay hands on you.” From that time on, they did not return on the Sabbath. (13:21).

Then I instructed the Levites to purify themselves and guard the gates in order to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember me for this as well, O my God, and show me mercy according to Your abundant loving devotion. (13:22).
In those days I also saw Jews who had married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. (13:23).
Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod or of the other peoples, but could not speak the language of Judah. (13:24).

I rebuked them and called down curses on them. I beat some of these men and pulled out their hair. Then I made them take an oath before God and said, “You must not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters as wives for your sons or for yourselves! (13:25).

Did not King Solomon of Israel sin in matters like this? There was not a king like him among many nations, and he was loved by his God, who made him king over all Israel— yet foreign women drew him into sin. (13:26).
Must we now hear that you too are doing all this terrible evil and acting unfaithfully against our God by marrying foreign women?” (13:27).
Even one of the sons of Jehoiada son of Eliashib the high priest had become a son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite. Therefore I drove him away from me. (13:28).
Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites. (13:29).
Thus I purified the priests and Levites from everything foreign, and I assigned specific duties to each of the priests and Levites. (13:30).
I also arranged for contributions of wood at the appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, with favor. (13:31).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 23:3-6: No Ammonite or Moabite is to enter the assembly, because they hired Balaam against Israel.
1 Kings 11:1-8: Solomon's foreign wives turn his heart after Ashtoreth and Milcom, the precedent Nehemiah names by name.
Malachi 3:8-10: Robbing God in tithes and offerings, and the command to bring the full tithe into the storehouse.
Jeremiah 17:19-27: Do not carry a load through the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath or bring it out of your houses.
Nehemiah 10:28-39: The signed obligations of the covenant that this chapter finds broken one by one.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לִשְׁכָּה גְדוֹלָה (lishkah gedolah, a large chamber)
translationNotes.note: Eliashib the priest, in charge of the temple chambers and related to Tobiah by marriage, cleared out a large storeroom and gave it to him as an apartment (13:4-5). That room had held the grain offering, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes of grain, wine and oil owed to the Levites. Nehemiah throws Tobiah's furniture into the street, has the rooms purified, and puts the stores back.

translationNotes.term: The Levites had gone back to their fields
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִישׁ־לְשָׂדֵהוּ (ish le-sadehu, each man to his field)
translationNotes.note: Levites were given no tribal allotment of land (Numbers 18:20-24; Deuteronomy 18:1-2). They lived on the tithe, holding only houses and pasture in forty-eight assigned towns (Numbers 35:1-8; Joshua 21). When the tithe stopped arriving, the singers and Levites walked off to farm, and the temple service simply stopped for lack of staff (13:10-11).

translationNotes.term: The men of Tyre and their fish
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הַצֹּרִים (hatsorim, the Tyrians)
translationNotes.note: Verse 16 has Tyrians living in Jerusalem bringing in fish and every kind of merchandise and selling it on the sabbath. Tyre was the Phoenician port about a hundred miles north, and Phoenician traders ran the salted-fish trade down the coast; Jerusalem's Fish Gate is named for that market (Zephaniah 1:10). Judeans were treading winepresses and loading donkeys on the same day (13:15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּאֲשֶׁר צָלֲלוּ שַׁעֲרֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם (ka'asher tsalalu sha'arei Yerushalayim, when the gates began to be dark)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew day runs sunset to sunset, so Nehemiah has the doors shut as the shadows fall before the sabbath and kept shut until it is over (13:19). Traders camped outside the wall once or twice to wait him out, and he threatened to lay hands on them. Then he stationed Levites at the gates for the day, because guarding a gate on the sabbath is priestly work.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וָאֶמְרְטֵם (va-emretem, and I pulled out their hair)
translationNotes.note: In 13:25 Nehemiah contends with the offenders, curses them, strikes some of them and pulls out their hair, then makes them swear by God about their children's marriages. Compare Ezra, who tore out his own hair over the same offence (Ezra 9:3). Both acts are public shaming, and the difference between the two men is exactly this: one turns the shame on himself, the other on the guilty.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַשְׁדּוֹדִית (ashdodit)
translationNotes.note: Half the children of these marriages spoke Ashdodite and could not speak Judean, that is, Hebrew (13:24). Ashdod was a Philistine city on the coast, and its people kept a distinct language into the Persian period. Once a generation cannot understand the language the Law is read in, the reading in Nehemiah 8 stops working.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וָאַבְרִיחֵהוּ מֵעָלָי (va-avrichehu me-alai, so I chased him from me)
translationNotes.note: A son of Joiada, son of Eliashib the high priest, had married the daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, which put the governor of Samaria one marriage away from the high priesthood in Jerusalem (13:28). Nehemiah expels him. The last verses of the book are a governor asking God to remember him for cleaning up a system he had already fixed once.

stories.keyTakeaway: When the Book of Moses is read, the people exclude all of foreign descent; Nehemiah returns from the king, throws Tobiah’s goods out of the temple room Eliashib had prepared for him, restores the Levites’ neglected portions, shuts the gates of Jerusalem against Sabbath trading, and confronts Jews married to foreign women, driving away a son of Jehoiada son of Eliashib the high priest who had become son-in-law to Sanballat.

intro:
Nehemiah was written by Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, the cupbearer-turned-governor whose first-person memoir forms the bulk of the book (Nehemiah 1:1-7:5; 12:27-43; 13:4-31, opening with "the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah" or "I, Nehemiah"). The book reached its final form in post-exilic Jerusalem around 430-400 BC, shortly after the events of Nehemiah's two governorships. Nehemiah was a Jew born and raised in Persia during the exile, serving as cupbearer (royal taster and confidant) to King Artaxerxes I in the winter capital of Susa, a position of high trust within the Persian court. In the twentieth year of Artaxerxes (445 BC), having received news that the walls of Jerusalem were still in ruins, he requested and received royal permission and letters of safe conduct to travel to Jerusalem as governor (Tirshatha) of the Persian province of Yehud. He served two governorships: the first from 445 to 433 BC (during which the city walls were rebuilt in fifty-two days despite opposition from Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arab) and a second after returning briefly to Persia. Tradition holds that Nehemiah also completed the closing genealogies of Chronicles after Ezra's death. Nehemiah and Ezra were contemporaries in Jerusalem during the first governorship and worked together on the reforms of the post-exilic community. The events of the book cover roughly 445 to 425 BC. The historical setting is the late Persian period under the Achaemenid Empire, with Yehud administered as a small satrapy from Jerusalem and surrounded by neighboring provinces (Samaria to the north under Sanballat, Ammon to the east under Tobiah, the Arabian territories to the south). Susa, where Nehemiah served, was one of four royal capitals of Persia (along with Persepolis, Ecbatana, and Babylon). Greece was at the height of its Classical period (the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta began in 431 BC); Egypt was a Persian satrapy under the 27th Dynasty, restive and soon to revolt.

Nehemiah is the sixteenth book of the Christian Old Testament. In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were originally counted as a single book within the Ketuvim (Writings); the Greek Septuagint translators distinguished them as Esdras B (Ezra) and a separate Esdras (Nehemiah), and the Latin Vulgate separated them into two distinct books, the arrangement inherited by English Bibles. The Hebrew title Nechemyah means "Yah comforts" or "Yahuah has comforted." Hebrew manuscript fragments of Nehemiah were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the Persian period or shortly after.
